entries.meaning: Before him the king saw Kaikeyī burning with fierce anger, as if Wrath had drawn its sword. Bad counsel was the hilt, cruelty the blade and the hunchback had whetted it upon the stone. Seeing it terrible and hard, the king wondered whether truth would take his life. Making his heart firm, he spoke humbly in words pleasing to her: ‘Beloved, why speak such harmful words, striking down courage, trust and love? Bharata and Rāma are my two eyes—I speak truth with Śaṅkara as witness. At dawn I shall certainly send messengers; on hearing, both brothers will come quickly. Finding an auspicious day and preparing everything, I shall publicly give Bharata the kingdom. Rāma has no greed for sovereignty and loves Bharata greatly. I had merely been following royal policy by considering elder and younger in my heart.’

The king continued, ‘Swearing by Rāma, I truthfully tell you that Rāma's mother said nothing to anyone. I did everything without asking you; therefore my plan has come to nothing. Abandon anger and now arrange auspicious things. After some days Bharata shall be heir apparent. Only one thing pains me: you asked for such a perplexing second boon. Even now my heart burns from its heat. Is this anger a jest or truly true? Tell me, abandoning wrath, what Rāma's offence is; everyone says Rāma is supremely virtuous. You too praise and love him, but hearing you now has filled me with doubt. One whose nature is favourable even to an enemy—how could he act adversely toward his mother? Beloved, abandon this joking anger and ask with reflective discernment for something by which I may behold Bharata's royal anointing to my eyes' content.’

Daśaratha pleaded, ‘A fish might live without water, and a miserable serpent might live without its jewel, but I speak without deceit in my heart: there is no life for me without Rāma. Understand this in your heart, discerning beloved—my life depends upon seeing Rāma.’ Hearing his gentle words, the malicious woman burned more intensely, as when clarified butter falls as an offering into fire. She said, ‘Try crores of measures if you wish; your māyā will not work here. Either give the boons or accept disgrace—I do not enjoy elaborate contrivance. Rāma is virtuous, you are virtuous and wise, and Rāma's mother is good—I have understood everyone. As Kauśalyā wished my welfare, I shall return that same fruit to her with force. If at daybreak Rāma does not go to the forest in ascetic dress, my death and your disgrace will follow. King, understand this within your mind.’

Speaking thus, the crooked woman rose and stood like a swelling river of wrath. That river emerged from the mountain of sin, filled with the water of anger beyond measure. The two boons were its banks, obstinacy its hard current, and the hunchback's words its whirlpool. Uprooting the tree that was the king, it flowed favourably toward the ocean of calamity. The king understood the statement to be fully true; Death danced upon his head in a woman's guise. Clasping Kaikeyī's feet, he pleaded and seated her: ‘Do not become an axe to the solar line. Ask for my head and I shall give it now, but do not kill me through separation from Rāma. Preserve Rāma by any means; otherwise my breast will burn throughout life.’ Seeing the disease incurable, the king fell to the ground, beating his head and crying in supreme anguish, ‘Rāma! Rāma! Lord of Raghu!’

The distraught king's whole body grew slack, as if a she-elephant had felled a wish-fulfilling tree. His throat dried and no word reached his mouth, like a wretched fish without water. Kaikeyī spoke again in harsh bitterness, as though putting poison into a wound: ‘If this was how you would act in the end, on whose strength did you keep saying, “Ask, ask”? Can two opposite things exist at once, king—laughing aloud and puffing one's cheeks? Can one be called generous while practising miserliness, or can boasting bring welfare? Either abandon the promise or hold courage; do not show compassion like a helpless woman. Body, wife, sons, home, wealth and land are described as straw to one bound to truth.’ Hearing words that pierced his vital place, the king said, ‘Speak; there is no fault of yours. Time, renowned as a demon, has possessed you and fallen upon me.’

The king said, ‘Bharata would never desire kingship; under Fate's control, evil judgment has entered your heart. All this is the outcome of my sin—Fate has struck at a bad place and become adverse. Ayodhyā will again dwell happily under the majesty of Rāma, abode of every virtue. All the brothers will serve him, and Rāma's greatness will fill the three worlds. Your stain and my remorse will not be erased even after death, nor will they leave anyone's memory. Now do whatever seems good to you. Sit beyond my sight and hide your face. As long as I live, I plead with joined hands, say nothing further. In the end you will regret it, unfortunate woman, like one who kills a cow in longing for leather.’ Having pleaded in crores of ways, the king collapsed, asking why she caused his destruction. Skilled in deception, she said nothing and kept vigil like a cremation ground.

The distraught king repeated ‘Rāma, Rāma’ like a helpless bird without wings. In his heart he prayed that dawn not come and that no one go tell Rāma. ‘Do not rise, sun, teacher of Raghu's line; seeing Ayodhyā will bring agony to your heart.’ The king's love and Kaikeyī's hardness were the two limits Fate had deliberately fashioned. Dawn came while the king lamented; vīṇās, lutes and conches sounded at the door. Bards recited and singers praised his virtues, but each sound struck the king like an arrow. How could any auspicious thing please him? It was like jewellery upon a woman about to enter her husband's funeral fire. No one slept that night, in eagerness and longing to see Rāma. Seeing the sun rise, the crowd of servants and ministers at the gate wondered: ‘The lord of Ayodhyā has not yet awakened—what special cause can there be?’

‘The king always wakes in the last watch; today this seems greatly strange to us. Go, Sumantra, awaken him and carry out the work upon receiving his command.’ Sumantra went inside the royal residence, but what he saw frightened even one accustomed to fear. It seemed Calamity and Despair had established a dwelling that threatened to devour whoever approached. No one answered his questions, so he went to the chamber where the king and Kaikeyī were. Offering the victory greeting, he bowed his head and sat; seeing the king's condition, he withered. The king lay pale and distraught with care upon the floor, like a lotus torn from its root. The frightened minister could not ask. Kaikeyī—full of ill omen and empty of good—spoke: ‘The king did not sleep at night; only the lord of the world knows why. Repeating “Rāma, Rāma,” he brought on dawn, but he does not tell his secret.’

Kaikeyī ordered, ‘Bring Rāma here quickly; when he arrives, ask the news.’ Understanding the king's inclination, Sumantra departed and realized the queen had devised some intrigue. Distraught with worry, his feet faltered on the road: ‘What will the king say after summoning Rāma?’ Gathering courage, he reached the gate, where everyone saw his downcast face and questioned him. Reassuring them all, he went where the ornament of the solar line was. Rāma saw Sumantra approaching and honoured him as a father. Saying it was the king's command, the minister took Rāma, lamp of Raghu's line, with him. Seeing Rāma going with the minister in such an ominous manner, people lamented everywhere. On arriving, the jewel of Raghu's line saw the king in an utterly wretched state. He recoiled in alarm like an aged elephant fallen before a lioness.

The king's lips were dry and every limb burned, like a wretched serpent deprived of its jewel. Seeing angry Kaikeyī nearby was like seeing Death counting down the hours. By his compassionate and gentle nature Rāma had never before seen sorrow or even heard it from anyone. Nevertheless, discerning the moment and holding firm, he asked his mother in sweet words: ‘Mother, tell me the cause of Father's grief so that whatever effort removes it may be made.’ Kaikeyī replied, ‘Hear the whole reason, Rāma. The king has very great love for you. He promised me two boons; I asked for whatever pleased me. Hearing it, worry entered the king's heart; because of regard for you, he cannot abandon it. Here is the king's difficulty: affection for his son on one side and his pledged word on the other. Can you not place his command upon your head and remove this grievous anguish?’
